text: I soon noticed that Bartleby never went to dinner, never went anywhere at all, and seemed to live on ginger nuts, which Ginger Nut brought him in exchange for a few coins. <break time="0.8s" /> One Sunday morning, on my way to Trinity Church, I stopped at my office and, to my surprise, found the door locked from within, and there appeared the lean face of Bartleby. <break time="0.8s" /> Standing in his shirt sleeves, he quietly told me that he was deeply engaged just then and that I had better walk round the block two or three times. <break time="0.8s" /> When I returned, he was gone, and from a blanket under his desk, a basin, a little soap, and a few crumbs of cheese, I saw that he had made my office his home. <break time="0.8s" /> Wall Street on a Sunday is as deserted as the ancient ruins of Petra, and the thought of his utter loneliness there, night after night, seized me with a fraternal melancholy. <break time="0.8s" /> Just in proportion as his forlornness grew in my imagination, did that pity merge into fear, for I perceived that it was his soul that suffered, and his soul I could not reach. <break time="0.8s" /> Strangely enough, my clerks and even I myself had begun to use the word prefer upon all sorts of occasions, and I trembled to think that contact with the scrivener had already affected me in a mental way. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, one day, Bartleby announced that he had given up copying altogether, and when I asked why, he answered only, Do you not see the reason for yourself.
